notes.headline: CrowdStrike posts record new recurring revenue and agrees to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal
notes.takeaway: Net new annual recurring revenue hit a record $419 million, up 58%, and ending ARR grew 27% to $6.26 billion as growth accelerated for a fifth straight quarter. CrowdStrike also agreed to acquire Zscaler for about $43.9 billion in stock; its shares fell 8.9% on the day.
results: Revenue rose 28% to $1.58 billion, with subscription revenue up 29% to $1.50 billion. Annual recurring revenue reached $6.26 billion, up 27%, and the company added a record $419.2 million of net new ARR in the quarter. Non-GAAP subscription gross margin was 82%.

On a GAAP basis CrowdStrike roughly broke even, with net income of $24.9 million ($0.02 per share), against a loss a year earlier. Non-GAAP operating income rose to $405.5 million and non-GAAP earnings per share to $0.34 from $0.24. Cash flow from operations was a record $665 million and free cash flow a record $474 million.
mgmt: Chief executive George Kurtz called it the best quarter in CrowdStrike’s history, saying customers are consolidating on the Falcon platform through the Falcon Flex licensing model, and that Falcon Guardian, which secures AI agents, passed $100 million of ARR in its first year. The company raised its full-year net new ARR growth guidance by 10.6 percentage points to about 45%.

Under the deal, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. Chief financial officer Burt Podbere said the acquisition should add to free cash flow per share immediately after closing, before any cost savings, and to revenue growth, operating margin and free cash flow margin within the first year after closing once synergies are included.
view: The quarter itself was excellent: accelerating ARR growth at this scale is rare in software, and it confirms that CrowdStrike recovered fully from the July 2024 outage. The deal is the bigger story. Buying Zscaler adds the leading cloud network security platform, which CrowdStrike lacked, and creates the broadest security company in the market.

Investors sold the shares 8.9% on the day, to $208.97, for good reasons: it is an all-stock deal that dilutes existing holders substantially, and combining two founder-led companies with different cultures is hard. At about 136 times forward earnings, CrowdStrike already traded at a large premium, and paying in its own richly valued stock is efficient for the buyer but leaves little room for error.

I think the strategic logic is strong, because customers want fewer security vendors and the two products barely overlap. The question is execution and regulators. If integration goes smoothly, the combined company should grow faster than either alone; if it stumbles, the premium valuation leaves a long way to fall. I would hold rather than add until the deal terms clear regulators.
notes.watch: Regulatory review of the Zscaler deal, net new ARR growth in the fourth quarter, and any customer churn from the combination.
